body.objective: Students will be able to accept and build offers.
body.iCan: I can accept and build offers.
successCriteria: I can accept my partner's offers
I can build on offers by adding new information
I can commit to a character with a clear objective
body.hook: The golden rule of improv comes from comedy theatres like The Second City in Toronto and Chicago: "Yes, and." Say no to your partner's idea and the scene dies. Say "yes, and" and the scene can go anywhere.

vocabulary.definition: Acting without a script, creating the scene in the moment.
Anything a performer says or does that gives the scene information.
To treat a partner's offer as true in the scene.
To reject or ignore an offer, which stops the scene.
What a character wants in a scene.
Fully believing in and playing your choices.

study.title: Yes, And
study.question: How do improvisers build a scene together without a script?
study.passage:
Warm-up, Word at a time story (5 minutes): In a circle, tell a story one word per person. Keep it moving.
Game 1, "No, but" vs "Yes, and" (10 minutes): In pairs, Partner A suggests a plan for a trip. Round 1: B answers every line with "No, but..." Round 2: B answers every line with "Yes, and..." Compare how each round felt.
Game 2, Gift giving (10 minutes): A mimes handing B a box. B opens it and names what's inside ("A live penguin!"). A accepts and adds ("I knew you'd love him, he needs feeding every hour").
Game 3, Objective scenes (20 minutes): Pairs draw a location card (bus stop, hospital waiting room, campsite) and each secretly draws an objective (get the other person to leave, borrow money, confess a secret). Improvise for two minutes using "Yes, and," pursuing your objective without blocking.
Debrief: Which offers moved the scene forward? Where did someone block?
study.source: Original activities written for this lesson; "yes, and" is a widely used improvisation principle.
steps: Warm up with a word-at-a-time story
discussion: How did "No, but" change the energy of the scene?
Which offer in your scene was the most useful? Why?
How can you pursue your objective without blocking your partner?
What makes an audience believe an improvised scene?
study.product: Perform a three-minute improvised scene with a partner from audience suggestions, then write a short reflection identifying two offers you accepted and how you built on them.

examples.title: Accepting
examples.problem: A says, "Captain, the ship is sinking!" What is an accepting response?
examples.answer: "Then grab the treasure map, I'm not leaving without it!"
examples.explore: What would a block sound like?

examples.title: Blocking
examples.problem: Identify the block: A: "Your dragon looks hungry." B: "I don't have a dragon."

examples.title: Objective
examples.problem: Your objective is to borrow money. Give a tactic.
examples.answer: Flatter: "You're the most generous person I know..."
examples.explore: What tactic could you switch to if this fails?

examples.title: Commitment
examples.problem: Why should you commit to a silly offer?
examples.answer: Full commitment makes the audience believe and enjoy the scene
examples.explore: What happens if you laugh and break character?

practice.a: Anything said or done that gives the scene information.
Accept the offer and add to it.

practice.q: Why does blocking stop a scene?
practice.a: It removes information and leaves nowhere to go.

practice.q: Give an example of building on the offer "It's freezing in here."
practice.a: "Because you left the igloo door open again!"
The way a character tries to get what they want.

practice.q: How can objectives create conflict without blocking?
practice.a: Characters want different things but accept each other's reality.
Fully believing in and playing your choices.

practice.q: Why listen more than you talk in improv?
practice.a: Your partner's offers give you material.

practice.q: How is disagreeing in character different from blocking?
practice.a: A character can disagree while still accepting the facts of the scene.

practice.q: Why does improv help scripted actors?
practice.a: It builds listening, spontaneity and truthful reactions.

practice.q: What should you do if your partner makes an offer you didn't expect?
practice.a: Accept it and find a way to build on it.

practice.q: How can status change during an improvised scene?
practice.a: One character gains or loses power through actions and words.

misconceptions: Thinking a character can't disagree without blocking
Planning a whole scene in advance instead of listening
exitTicket: Respond with "Yes, and" to: "This is the strangest restaurant I've ever seen."
Name one objective and one tactic.

test.title: Practice test: Accept and build offers

items.q: Improvisation is
items.answer: C) acting without a script

items.q: An offer is
options: D) information given to the scene
items.answer: D) information given to the scene

items.q: "Yes, and" means
items.answer: B) accept and add

items.q: An objective is
items.answer: B) what a character wants

items.q: Which line blocks the offer "Let's climb the mountain"?
options: D) "Only if we reach the top by sunset."
items.answer: A) "There's no mountain."

items.q: A tactic is
options: B) how a character tries to get what they want
D) a line of dialogue only
items.answer: B) how a character tries to get what they want

items.q: Commitment in improv means
options: C) fully believing in your choices
items.answer: C) fully believing in your choices

items.q: Why does blocking hurt a scene?
options: A) It adds too much detail
C) It removes information and stalls the action
D) It makes the scene longer
items.answer: C) It removes information and stalls the action

items.q: The best way to find your next line in improv is to
options: B) plan it before the scene
D) listen to your partner's offer
items.answer: D) listen to your partner's offer

items.q: A character can disagree without blocking by
options: A) accepting the facts but wanting something different
items.answer: A) accepting the facts but wanting something different

items.q: Improv helps scripted actors mainly by building
items.answer: C) listening and truthful reactions

items.q: If your partner makes an unexpected offer, you should
options: C) accept it and build on it
items.answer: C) accept it and build on it

items.q: Define offer.
items.answer: Information given to the scene by a performer.

items.q: What does blocking mean in improv?
items.answer: Rejecting or ignoring an offer.

items.q: Build on the offer: "Doctor, my nose is glowing."
items.answer: Answers vary; accepts and adds.

items.q: Explain the difference between an objective and a tactic.
items.answer: The objective is what you want; a tactic is how you try to get it.

items.q: Why is commitment important in improv?
items.answer: It makes the scene believable and engaging.

items.q: Give one reason "No, but" scenes struggle.
items.answer: Ideas keep getting rejected so the scene can't build.

items.q: Explain how a character can disagree without blocking.
items.answer: Accept the reality of the scene but pursue a different objective.

items.q: Describe how improv skills help in scripted scenes.
items.answer: Listening, reacting truthfully and recovering from mistakes.
